opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it comes down to the difference between answering a question and creating the space in which a whole family of questions can even be asked.

When someone proves a difficult theorem, say Fermat's Last Theorem, it's an extraordinary achievement. But in some sense the target was already there. People knew what they were aiming at. The question was well-posed, and the challenge was finding a path to it, which can take enormous ingenuity and centuries of failed attempts. It's like summiting a mountain everyone can see.

Inventing a new branch of mathematics is different. Think of Newton and Leibniz with calculus, or Cantor with set theory and transfinite numbers, or Shannon with information theory. Before them, people didn't just lack the answers; they lacked the concepts needed to frame the questions. They're not climbing a known mountain. They're revealing a whole new mountain range that nobody knew was there, and then everyone else gets to spend generations exploring it.

There's also a counterfactual element that I find quite compelling. With a famous open problem, many brilliant people are working on it, so if one person hadn't solved it, there's a decent chance someone else would have before long. With a genuinely new field, it often requires a particular kind of vision: seeing that some vague, informal idea like "information" or "infinity" or "probability" could be made precise and fruitful. That's rarer, and the downstream value is much larger, because a single new framework can generate thousands of theorems, including many hard ones.

So I'd say proving a hard theorem shows tremendous skill, but founding a field shows a kind of creative insight that changes what's possible for everyone who comes after. And as someone interested in how ideas shape the long-term future, that kind of contribution, opening up new territory rather than settling a single point within it, strikes me as the more impressive and often the more valuable.

r001.rationale: It says inventing a branch creates the space for a family of questions and provides concepts needed to frame questions that could not previously be asked.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it comes down to what each achievement tells you about the space of possibilities. When someone proves a difficult theorem, the question was already there. Fermat's Last Theorem sat on the table for three and a half centuries, and everyone agreed on what it would mean to settle it. Proving it took extraordinary skill and persistence, and I don't want to diminish that. But the problem was handed to the prover by history.

Inventing a branch of mathematics is different in kind, not just in degree. Think about Newton and Leibniz with the calculus, or Cantor with set theory, or Shannon with information theory. Before them, there wasn't a question waiting to be answered. There wasn't even a vocabulary in which the questions could be posed. They had to see that there was a structure there at all, carve out the right concepts, and then show that those concepts were fertile, that they opened onto hundreds of further problems that nobody could have formulated the week before.

So one way to put it is that proving a theorem moves you from one known point to another, along a path that was hard to find. Inventing a field adds a new dimension to the map. It changes what counts as a point. And the value compounds, because every subsequent theorem in that field is partly downstream of the person who made the field exist.

There's also an epistemic humility angle that I find interesting. When you look at a hard open problem, you can at least estimate how hard it is, because you know what you're up against. With a new branch of mathematics, we usually can't see in advance that it was even available to be invented. That's part of why these things look so much like genius in retrospect. The person had to notice an absence that nobody else experienced as an absence.

And I think that matters when we think about the long-term future more broadly. A lot of what's most valuable in human history isn't solving the problems in front of us but expanding the set of things we're able to think about at all. The invention of new frameworks, whether in mathematics or ethics or science, is probably where a large share of our potential actually lives.

r001.rationale: The response says a new branch creates a vocabulary for questions that could not previously be posed, and opens further problems no one could have formulated before.

astra-6.text:
Well, proving a difficult theorem can be an extraordinary achievement, but you’re usually working within an existing framework. You’ve got a question, and you’re trying to find a path to the answer. Inventing a new branch of mathematics involves seeing that there’s a whole set of questions worth asking that people hadn’t recognised before, and finding the concepts that let you ask them precisely.

What impresses me is that combination of imagination and judgment. You can invent arbitrary definitions, but creating something that turns out to be rich — that other mathematicians can spend generations exploring — is quite different. You’re not just solving a problem; you’re opening up possibilities for other people to discover things.

Of course, the distinction isn’t sharp. A proof of a difficult theorem can introduce ideas that effectively create a new field. So it’s really that ability to give us a new way of thinking that I find especially impressive.

r001.rationale: It says inventing a branch reveals questions people had not recognized and provides concepts to formulate them precisely.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, proving a difficult theorem can require extraordinary ingenuity, but you’re usually working within a framework that someone has already given you. You know what the objects are, what the question is, and what would count as an answer. Inventing a new branch of mathematics involves seeing that there’s a fruitful framework there in the first place.

You have to find the right concepts and definitions — ones that capture something interesting and allow other people to make progress. You can define endlessly many mathematical structures, but most of them won’t lead anywhere. Finding one that opens up a whole landscape of important questions seems to me a particularly profound kind of creativity.

And it can enable much more than any single result. Other mathematicians can spend generations exploring what you’ve opened up. That doesn’t mean it’s always harder than proving a theorem, but it’s that ability to create a new way of thinking that I find especially impressive.

r001.rationale: The response says a new branch opens up a landscape of questions, but does not clearly say those questions could not previously be formulated.
